reconcile.connective: Gill reads 1 Timothy 2:1's "all men" as "men of all sorts," excepting those who have "sinned the sin unto death" — Jeremiah's very case.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible sets the verses side by side as a bare Yes/No pair — the command to pray for all against three divine bans on praying for Judah — without offering a harmonization.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Should you pray for everyone?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/pray_for_everyone.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Should you pray for everyone?"

excerpts.excerpt_text: nor is prayer to be made for such who have sinned the sin unto death, Jo1 5:16 … But the words must be understood of men of all sorts, of every rank and quality, as the following verse shows.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly limits 1 Tim 2:1's 'all men' to 'men of all sorts' rather than a distributive every-individual reading, explicitly carving out an exception for those who have 'sinned the sin unto death' (1 John 5:16) — the very category Gill's own notes on Jeremiah 11:13 and 14:11 place Judah in — dissolving the apparent universalism.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on 1 Timothy 2:1
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this exact tension, reading 1 Timothy 2:1's 'all men' as 'men of all sorts' rather than every individual and explicitly excepting those who have 'sinned the sin unto death' (1 John 5:16) — the same category into which his parallel notes on Jeremiah 11:13-14 and 14:11 place Judah, where the prohibition is read as barring prayer only for their temporal deliverance, not their eternal salvation. (Haley's scripture index lists no entry for Jeremiah 7:16, 11:14, 14:11, or 1 Timothy 2:1; per spec a row-surfaced harmonizing commentator keyed to the passage is used instead.)
